channel.title: The Machine and the Grid
channel.description: A single-narrator documentary series on the technologies reshaping computing and energy. Each season takes one subject and builds it from first principles: what AI is, what it runs on, what it does, and the electrical grid now straining to keep up with it.
channel.itunes:author: Liam Norris
channel.itunes:subtitle: How artificial intelligence actually works, and what it takes to power it.
channel.itunes:summary: A single-narrator documentary series on the technologies reshaping computing and energy. Each season takes one subject and builds it from first principles: what AI is, what it runs on, what it does, and the electrical grid now straining to keep up with it.

item.title: The AI Infrastructure Debate — 13. What Is Everyone Missing
item.description: The blind spots neither host sees discussed enough, led by the one that changed how the other thinks: the grid's markets and physics were never built for loads like this, and a redesign is coming that almost nobody is talking about.
item.itunes:summary: The blind spots neither host sees discussed enough, led by the one that changed how the other thinks: the grid's markets and physics were never built for loads like this, and a redesign is coming that almost nobody is talking about.

item.title: The AI Infrastructure Debate — 12. AI in 2040
item.description: Two pictures of 2040, each attacked by the host who painted it, with a hard line drawn between reasonable physical extrapolation and genuine guesses about human behavior.
item.itunes:summary: Two pictures of 2040, each attacked by the host who painted it, with a hard line drawn between reasonable physical extrapolation and genuine guesses about human behavior.

item.title: The AI Infrastructure Debate — 11. What If AI Doesn't Need That Many Data Centers
item.description: The bear's bear case. Better models, better chips, smaller models and edge computing all compound at once. What if efficiency outpaces demand growth and leaves an oversupply of infrastructure nobody needed?
item.itunes:summary: The bear's bear case. Better models, better chips, smaller models and edge computing all compound at once. What if efficiency outpaces demand growth and leaves an oversupply of infrastructure nobody needed?

item.title: The AI Infrastructure Debate — 10. The Great Data Center Shakeout
item.description: Merchant developers and the GPU-renting neoclouds are the stars of this cycle. A land rush this frantic has historically ended with a lot of the early rushers gone.
item.itunes:summary: Merchant developers and the GPU-renting neoclouds are the stars of this cycle. A land rush this frantic has historically ended with a lot of the early rushers gone.

item.title: The AI Infrastructure Debate — 9. Where Should AI Live
item.description: Training can run in the middle of nowhere next to a cheap power plant. Inference cannot. That split decides which regions become AI capitals, and hundreds of billions of dollars are choosing locations right now.
item.itunes:summary: Training can run in the middle of nowhere next to a cheap power plant. Inference cannot. That split decides which regions become AI capitals, and hundreds of billions of dollars are choosing locations right now.

item.title: The AI Infrastructure Debate — 8. Does AI Trigger a Natural Gas Renaissance
item.description: A deliberate role reversal. The energy realist argues gas wins because it is the only thing ready at scale on the timeline the buildout demands; the tech optimist calls it a trap dressed up as a bridge.
item.itunes:summary: A deliberate role reversal. The energy realist argues gas wins because it is the only thing ready at scale on the timeline the buildout demands; the tech optimist calls it a trap dressed up as a bridge.

item.title: The AI Infrastructure Debate — 7. Will Nuclear Finally Have Its Moment
item.description: Data centers want power that is clean, firm and dense, and exactly one technology is all three at once. Whether that finally breaks fifty years of nuclear stagnation is a different question.
item.itunes:summary: Data centers want power that is clean, firm and dense, and exactly one technology is all three at once. Whether that finally breaks fifty years of nuclear stagnation is a different question.

item.title: The AI Infrastructure Debate — 6. Grid vs. Behind the Meter
item.description: Connect through the utility and the shared grid, or build your own generation on site and skip the grid altogether? One of the most consequential engineering and business calls in the entire buildout, with serious money on both sides.
item.itunes:summary: Connect through the utility and the shared grid, or build your own generation on site and skip the grid altogether? One of the most consequential engineering and business calls in the entire buildout, with serious money on both sides.

item.title: The AI Infrastructure Debate — 5. Power, the New Oil
item.description: Electricity went from a line item nobody thought about to the first question anyone asks about a new AI campus. Whether power is now the constraint that decides who wins and who gets locked out.
item.itunes:summary: Electricity went from a line item nobody thought about to the first question anyone asks about a new AI campus. Whether power is now the constraint that decides who wins and who gets locked out.

item.title: The AI Infrastructure Debate — 4. Is Intelligence Becoming a Commodity
item.description: Inference costs are collapsing and free open-weight models are closing the gap. If intelligence becomes almost free, does that create enormous profit or eliminate it?
item.itunes:summary: Inference costs are collapsing and free open-weight models are closing the gap. If intelligence becomes almost free, does that create enormous profit or eliminate it?

item.title: The AI Infrastructure Debate — 3. Who Actually Makes the Money
item.description: Trillions moving through chips, clouds, models, apps, power and wires. Where does profit actually pool, and where does it just pass through on its way to the customer? The airline industry as a warning.
item.itunes:summary: Trillions moving through chips, clouds, models, apps, power and wires. Where does profit actually pool, and where does it just pass through on its way to the customer? The airline industry as a warning.

item.title: The AI Infrastructure Debate — 2. Is There an AI Bubble
item.description: Can AI be genuinely revolutionary and a financial bubble at the same time? In most people's heads those are opposites. Historically they are best friends.

item.title: The AI Infrastructure Debate — 1. Is AI Worth Trillions
item.description: The opening question: can AI generate enough revenue to justify the capital being poured into it? They land on a split decision, probably yes for the world, not for everyone building it.

item.title: Who Runs the Grid — 4. The Patchwork and the Seams

item.title: Who Runs the Grid — 3. The Deal and the Great Unbundling
item.description: At the dawn of the electricity industry, in the early nineteen-hundreds, there was a real question about how this new business should be organized. And one of the most influential answers came from a man named Samuel Insull, a former secretary to Thomas Edison who built a power empire in Chicago.

item.title: The Agents — 4. The Long Leash
item.description: Imagine you hire a brilliant, eager, blazingly fast personal assistant. Total recall, works around the clock, does exactly what you ask. But this assistant has one strange flaw: they cannot tell the difference between an instruction from you and an instruction they read somewhere else.

item.description: For about forty years, the software business has worked one way. You pay for a seat. A license. The right for one person to use a tool. Your company buys a hundred seats of the accounting software, five hundred logins for the customer system, a subscription per employee per month.

item.title: The Agents — 2. The Ninety-Five Percent Problem
item.description: Let me give you a number that explains more about the last three years of A.I. than almost anything else, and it's just arithmetic. Suppose you've got an agent that's really good. On any single step of a task, it makes the right move ninety-five percent of the time. Nineteen times out of twenty.

item.title: The Agents — 1. The Loop
item.description: Picture a screen, and nobody at the keyboard. On that screen, a piece of software is working. It reads a file. It thinks for a moment. It runs a command, and the command fails, an error scrolls up in red. It reads the error. It pauses. It edits a line of code, runs the command again, and this time it works.

item.title: Bare Metal — 4. The Moat and the Commons
item.description: In January of 2025, a Chinese lab most Western investors had barely heard of released an A.I. model called DeepSeek. And it did two things at once that seemed almost contradictory. First, it was very good, competitive with the best models the giant American labs had spent billions to build. Second, they gave it away.

item.description: In the summer of 2024, a company took an old appliance factory outside Memphis, Tennessee, and in one hundred and twenty two days, not years, days, turned it into the most powerful A.I. supercomputer on earth. They called it Colossus.
